additions.description: צוֹם = תַּעֲנִית (fast = fasting — the nominal form equated with the practice)
additions.source_text_ref: Line 5: 'קָרֵי לֵהּ צוֹם וְקָרֵי לֵהּ שָׂשׂוֹן... כְּשֶׁאֵין שָׁלוֹם – צוֹם'. The teaching treats צוֹם and תַּעֲנִית as the same bechina throughout, but only צְדָקָה—תַּעֲנִית is encoded.
additions.notes: The text uses צוֹם and תַּעֲנִית interchangeably throughout. Encoding this bechina would explicitly confirm their identity and add the well-known Rabbinic category 'צוֹם' into Package 2. The phrase 'כְּשֶׁאֵין שָׁלוֹם – צוֹם' directly parallels 'לְבַטֵּל הַמַּחֲלֹקֶת...עַל זֶה צָרִיךְ תַּעֲנִית'. They are the same thing expressed through two synonyms.

additions.description: כָּבוֹד = רָצוֹן (honor/will of a person — the Yerushalmi equation cited in a parallel Torah)
additions.source_text_ref: The proof text used in edge ID 2778 (Torah 177, bechina: כבוד = רצון via Yerushalmi Pe'ah) is conceptually invoked in Torah 179 through the Zohar passage: the teaching equates subduing the נֶפֶשׁ/רָצוֹן with Yom Kippur's affliction. The Yerushalmi 'רְצוֹנוֹ שֶׁל אָדָם זֶהוּ כְּבוֹדוֹ' undergirds the argument but is not encoded for reference 179.
additions.notes: While this bechina is encoded for Torah 177 (edge ID 2778), the same concept operates implicitly in Torah 179: by subduing one's רָצוֹן before God's will (fasting), one's כָּבוֹד is ultimately elevated (marbeh tzedakah marbeh shalom). The Rebbe cites 'בַּטֵּל רְצוֹנְךָ מִפְּנֵי רְצוֹנוֹ' — which inherently invokes the כָּבוֹד = רָצוֹן equation. Priority medium because it is explicit in Torah 177 but only implicit here.

analysis_notes.nodes_in_dataset_not_in_packages: 8 nodes appear only in eitza edges for Torah 179. All are correctly excluded from packages per framework: they represent either the problem (strife), the intermediate states, or the positive outcomes of fasting — all of which are eitza relationships (cause and effect), not bechina identities. The framework correctly distinguishes: the NATURE of strife and fasting (bechina) from what fasting PRODUCES (eitza).

יוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים as the supreme/comprehensive תַּעֲנִית ('כְּלָלוּת כָּל הַיָּמִים') — the teaching implies Yom Kippur = the ultimate fasting-day that includes all others, but this is not encoded as a bechina edge

The Zohar's 'לְאַכְנָעָא לִבָּא לְאַדְבְּקָא רְעוּתָא דְּלִבָּא' — the inner attachment of the heart's will to God could be a bechina of תַּעֲנִית (fasting = attachment of will to God) but is presented as the mechanism/effect of fasting rather than its essential nature
כָּבוֹד = רָצוֹן (implicit from the Yerushalmi equation cited in parallel Torahs) — operates in the background of the teaching but not encoded for Torah 179
structural_observations: Torah 179 is among the most eitza-heavy Torahs in the dataset: of 14 total edges, only 3 are bechina and 11 are eitza. This reflects the teaching's character as practical advice (עֵצָה): here is what you do (fast) and here is what results (peace, joy).

The 3 bechina edges encode the three key conceptual identifications that undergird the entire teaching: (1) נֶפֶשׁ = רָצוֹן [what you are subduing], (2) מַחֲלֹקֶת = רְצוֹנוֹת אֲחֵרִים [what opposes you], (3) צְדָקָה = תַּעֲנִית [the practice and its merit are the same thing].

The teaching has a clean good/evil structure but it is expressed through eitza chains rather than bechina clusters: strife (evil, package 1 node) is defeated by fasting (good, package 2) producing peace and joy (good). The conceptual packages are thin because the Torah's real content is in its eitza architecture.

Package 1 (הָרָצוֹן) is marked neutral rather than good or evil because רָצוֹן itself is structurally neutral — it is the ground from which both holy will (נֶפֶשׁ aligned with God) and alien will (מַחֲלֹקֶת opposing you) arise. The teaching's practical wisdom is precisely this: recognize that strife is a will-phenomenon, subdue your own will before God (fasting), and the alien wills dissolve.
